dataset_family: Single-site Japanese older-adult sample from medical and nursing care facilities (Kyoto Tachibana University ethics 25-11; 2024-2025): 31 MCI and 43 cognitively healthy controls
method_family: Computerised visual reaction-time paradigm (central-field vs Useful-Field-of-View detection, VRAS) with head-mounted eye-tracking; t-tests, mixed ANOVA, ANCOVA, logistic regression/ROC
what_it_shows: A within-study loaded-versus-unloaded behavioural head-to-head in 31 MCI vs 43 age-comparable healthy controls. Central-field detection RT does not separate the groups (554.4 vs 568.5 ms, p = 0.228; central omission and commission errors also n.s.). UFOV RT does (580.3 vs 638.6 ms, p < 0.001, d = -1.17), with a formal Task x Group interaction (F(1,72) = 19.09, p < 0.001), and the group effect survives central RT as a covariate (F = 37.94). The loaded measure is a single peripheral-detection task under central fixation, not a dual task.
why: PDF identity confirmed: the map entry, DOI 10.1038/s41598-025-32034-6, title and authors (Tamaru, Inada, Ideguchi, Kagino, Katsuhara, Higashi) match the block. Read to the References. The study runs its own loaded-versus-unloaded comparison in the same participants against a matched non-impaired comparator (age p = 0.12). It also tests the interaction formally, which P-665/P-687 did not (they report two separate t-tests). Why partly and not yes: the statement names three families of loaded measure (diffusion microstructure, task-evoked electrophysiology, dual-task performance), and the UFOV task here is not a dual task. Per the Methods (p.3), participants held gaze on a central fixation point while detecting peripheral targets, with no concurrent central task. 'Divided attention' and 'dual-task interference' are the authors' Discussion interpretation (pp.6-7), not the design. The study fits only if the family list is read as illustrative rather than exhaustive; that is a decision for the operator, not a verifier. Confounds that weaken the dissociation: (a) fixed order, with the central task always first (p.3); (b) 20 central vs 80 UFOV trials (p.3); (c) targets sat 20 cm from centre at 1 m viewing distance, so peripheral RT carries retinal-eccentricity costs and possible gaze-shift costs. Visual orienting frequency (gaze shifts away from fixation) was higher in MCI at trend level (p = 0.052). No visual-field assessment is reported beyond excluding visual impairment and corrective-glasses users. (d) MCI and HC were defined only by MoCA-J/MMSE-J cut-offs, which the authors call provisional (p.7). (e) Single-site sample from care facilities. Independence: Kyoto single-site sample, with no overlap in site, cohort or authors with P-651, P-661, P-662, P-665/P-687 or P-666, or with P-522/P-633. The method family (behavioural RT with eye-tracking) is distinct from diffusion MRI, EEG and gait/TUG. Not a preprint (Scientific Reports 2026). supports_narrowed is n/a because the round-20 wording declares VF-25 not a convergence. For reference, the finding is of the same kind as the descriptive dual- vs single-task TUG dissociation that wording records, but the load is a single-task attentional (peripheral-field) load, not a dual task.

quotes.quote: Inclusion criteria for the HC group were a score of ≥ 26 on the Japanese version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA-J) and a score of 28–30 on the Japanese version of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE-J). The MCI group included patients with MoCA-J scores ≤ 25 and MMSE-J scores 24–27
To minimize potential carry-over effects, the central visual field task was always presented first, followed by the UFOV task.

Condition 2 (UFOV task): A black fixation point of the same size remained at the center of the screen. While maintaining gaze on the fixation point, red circular targets identical to those in Condition 1 were presented in one of four peripheral locations—upper right (45°), lower right (135°), lower left (225°), or upper left (315°)—each 20 cm from center.
The C-RT task consisted of 20 trials and the UFOV task consisted of 80 trials.

For central reaction time (C-RT), the HC group had a mean of 554.4 ms (SD = 46.6), and the MCI group had a mean of 568.5 ms (SD = 52.6). This difference was not statistically significant (t = − 1.22, p = 0.228, Cohen’s d = − 0.29). In contrast, for Useful-Field Reaction Time (U-RT), the HC group recorded a mean of 580.3 ms (SD = 44.9), while the MCI group had a significantly slower mean of 638.6 ms (SD = 38.4), indicating a significant group difference (t = − 5.84, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = − 1.17)

A mixed-design ANOVA with task condition (C-RT vs. U-RT) as the within-subject factor and group (HC vs. MCI) as the between-subject factor revealed a significant Task × Group interaction, F(1,72) = 19.09, p < 0.001
the group effect remained highly significant after controlling for C-RT, F(1,72) = 37.94, p < 0.001

For central omission errors (C-OE), the median was 0.0 in both groups (interquartile range [IQR]: 0.0–0.0), showing no between-group variability. The difference was not statistically significant (U = 745.5, Z = 1.276, p = 0.202, r = 0.148).

In the UFOV task, the MCI group exhibited a slightly higher VOF (median = 3.0, IQR 2.0–3.0) compared to the HC group (median = 2.0, IQR 2.0–3.0). This difference approached but did not reach statistical significance (U = 833.0, p = 0.052, r = 0.230)
These results are also interpretable within dual-task interference and attentional bottleneck frameworks, as originally proposed by Welford34 and Pashler35.

Third, MCI classification was based solely on MoCA and MMSE scores. While these are widely used screening tools, the gold standard typically involves a consensus clinical diagnosis incorporating multidisciplinary evaluation. Therefore, our classification should be considered provisional
